food.text: Mesopotamia is described as the site of the earliest developments of the Neolithic Revolution, from around 10,000 BC. It is credited with the planting of the first cereal crops, along with the invention of the wheel and the development of cursive script.
The Sumerians were one of the first known beer-drinking societies. Cereals were plentiful and were the key ingredient in their early brew, and they made wheat, barley and mixed grain beers.

Sumerian farmers grew an abundance of grain and other crops. The surplus enabled them to form urban settlements, and the world's earliest known texts come from the Sumerian cities of Uruk and Jemdet Nasr, dating to about 3350 to 2500 BC.

The Pre-Pottery Neolithic A period, from 10,000 to 8,700 BC, saw the introduction of agriculture in Mesopotamia. The oldest evidence for animal domestication dates to the transition from that period to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic B, at the end of the 9th millennium BC.
The Sumerians grew barley, chickpeas, lentils, wheat, dates, onions, garlic, lettuce, leeks and mustard. They also caught many fish and hunted fowl and gazelle.
The transition to animal domestication has been documented at sites like Abu Hureyra and Mureybet. Both continued to be occupied from the Natufian well into the Pre-Pottery Neolithic B.

Excavations revealed that Jarmo, in the foothills of the Zagros Mountains, was an agricultural community dating back to 7500 BC. Its farming was based on irrigation through natural rainfall. It was broadly contemporary with Jericho in the southern Levant.

The Hassuna culture, c. 6500 to 6000 BC, farmed in a rainy region where dry farming was possible. Its villagers grew a wide variety of grains, lentils and peas, raised cattle, goats, sheep and pigs, and hunted aurochs, gazelles and bears.

Beer brewing was so important to the Sumerians that it appears in the Epic of Gilgamesh. When Enkidu is introduced to the food and beer of Gilgamesh's people, he drinks seven jugs of beer and becomes expansive and sings with joy.

At Umm Dabaghiyah, occupied around 7000 to 6500 BC, people ran a mixed economy and hunted for skin and meat. Wheat, lentils and barley were present, and wall paintings suggest that fast-moving onagers were caught in nets.
The Samarra culture was the first to practice a primitive form of irrigation agriculture along the middle Tigris River and its tributaries, dating to about 5,700 to 4,900 BC.

At Kosak Shamali, an Ubaid site in northern Syria, the animal bones show a large share of domesticated sheep and goat. Changes in the bones suggest that secondary products such as wool and milk grew more important toward the late Ubaid and the Uruk period.

art.text: Around 8000 BC, before pottery was invented, several early settlements became experts at crafting beautiful, sophisticated stone containers. They used alabaster or granite, shaped and polished with sand. Artisans used the veins in the material to maximum visual effect.

Samarra culture pottery was easily recognizable and often elaborately decorated. Geometric designs were painted in bright red, brown, or purple-brown. The motifs could also represent men, women, birds, fish, antelopes, or scorpions.

The Hassuna culture of northern Mesopotamia dates to the early sixth millennium BC and is named after Tell Hassuna in Iraq. Its pottery decoration consists essentially of geometrical shapes, along with a few ibex designs.

The Uruk Trough is one of the oldest examples of narrative art. This limestone object shows flocks of sheep carved in relief approaching a reed hut, with lambs coming out of the structure. It could have functioned as a cult image in the temple of Inanna.

The Mask of Warka, also called the Lady of Warka, is a marble head of a goddess that most likely represents Inanna. Dating to circa 3100 BCE, it is probably from one of the earliest known near life-size sculptures. Its face was most likely inlaid with precious stones such as lapis lazuli.

Such stone containers have been found in abundance on the upper Euphrates river, in what is today eastern Syria. The site of Bouqras is especially notable. These objects form the early stages of the development of the art of Mesopotamia.

Samarra pottery was documented at Tell es-Sawwan and Choga Mami in central Mesopotamia. It consists of large bowls and vases with rounded shoulders, made of a light beige, slightly rough material. Some necklaces even have reliefs of human faces with stylized features.

At Uruk, small animal figurines were offered as votives, in a style mixing naturalistic and abstract elements to capture the animal's spiritual essence. They probably replaced a ritual act of animal sacrifice by leaving the image of the sacrificed animal in the temple. Many were found at Uruk Level III, circa 3000 BCE.

In Temple C in the Eanna District at Uruk, excavators found pillars containing cone mosaic panels, dated to around 3300 to 3000 BCE. Ten-centimeter cones of baked clay or gypsum were pressed into wet plaster and painted. They formed diamond, triangle, and zigzag patterns.
The Mask of Warka was discovered in the Eanna district at Uruk. The head once belonged to a larger composite statue of the goddess, which was most likely made out of wood.

war.text: Around 8000 BCE, the people of Jericho built a massive stone wall and tower during the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A period. This fortification system has led UNESCO to recognize Jericho as the oldest fortified city in the world.

Excavations in 2005 and 2006 showed that the ancient city of Hamoukar in northeastern Syria was destroyed around 3500 BCE, possibly in the earliest urban warfare attested in the Near East's archaeological record. Slings and thousands of clay bullets were found, indicating a siege, along with widespread signs of destruction. Who destroyed it is uncertain, but the city may have fallen victim to the Uruk expansion from the south, since the next occupation layer is of the Uruk civilization. The city had been one of the largest in Northern Mesopotamia, covering about 105 hectares.

Long before its destruction, Hamoukar was a major center for producing obsidian weapons and tools, with volcanic glass imported from around Mount Nemrut in modern Turkey, some 170 kilometers to the north. Chemical analysis confirmed this distant origin, since no obsidian occurs naturally near Hamoukar itself.

Raising Jericho's early wall and tower would have required about a hundred workers laboring for more than a hundred days. This points to an unusually organized community already existing during the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A period.

Hamoukar's obsidian workshops sat in the city's lower town and had been producing weapons and tools for centuries before the city's destruction around 3500 BCE. This organized craft production shows sophisticated economic activity well before that final catastrophe.

Despite its scale, Jericho's wall may not have been built against human enemies at all. Some archaeologists think it defended against floodwater and soil erosion, while the adjoining tower served a ceremonial rather than a military role.

The discovery of independent obsidian weapon production at Hamoukar surprised archaeologists. It revealed a trading network in northern Mesopotamia that operated outside the influence of southern cities such as Ur and Uruk.

Radiocarbon dates show Jericho's stone tower was built around 8300 BCE and stayed in use until about 7800 BCE. That means the tower remained an active part of the settlement for centuries before eventually falling into disuse.

science.text: Mesopotamia is the site of the earliest developments of the Neolithic Revolution, from around 10,000 BC. It has been credited with inspiring the invention of the wheel, the planting of the first cereal crops, cursive script, mathematics, astronomy, and agriculture.

The earliest dates for the actual domestication of animals are c. 9000 BCE for goats and sheep, c. 8500 BCE for pigs, and c. 8000 BCE for cattle. All of these come from the area of Northern Mesopotamia.

Sumerian technology is credited with the wheel, cuneiform script, arithmetic and geometry, irrigation systems, Sumerian boats, and a lunisolar calendar. The list also includes bronze, saws, chisels, hammers, nails, glue and beer.

It is believed that the use of clay plaster for floors and walls during the Pre-Pottery Neolithic B led to the discovery of pottery. The earliest proto-pottery was White Ware, made from lime and gray ash built up around baskets before firing. It was made for several centuries around 7000 BC at sites such as Tell Neba'a Faour in the Beqaa Valley.

Evidence for early wool production is ambiguous and mostly indirect. The domestication of sheep and goat started in the ninth millennium BC, and wool-bearing sheep are clearly attested in Uruk-period sites. Exactly when wool production emerged between those two points is unclear.

Managing temple accounts within an organized agricultural system led the Sumerians to develop writing, around 3500 BC. That system included organized irrigation, plough agriculture and a specialized labour force under bureaucratic control.

The Samarra period (c. 6200–5700 BC) brought architectural innovations such as tripartite houses, along with the earliest evidence of irrigation canals. It is known especially from Tell es-Sawwan and Choga Mami in central Mesopotamia.

During the Hassuna period, in the second half of the 7th millennium BC, sites such as Hassuna, Yarim Tepe and Telul eth-Thalathat show more complex house plans. They also show the introduction of collective granaries.

Cylinder seals were invented in Mesopotamia in the early 4th millennium BCE, in the Uruk period, as an evolutionary step from accounting systems and seals going back to the early 7th millennium BCE. In Egypt they appear suddenly from around Naqada II c-d (3500–3300 BCE), with designs clearly inspired by those of Mesopotamia.

One theory holds that the Samarra culture was the first to practice a primitive form of irrigation agriculture along the middle Tigris River. Farming peoples then spread down into southern Mesopotamia because they had developed a temple-centered social organization for mobilizing labor and technology for water control. The link is most clearly seen at Tell el-'Oueili near Larsa.

politics.text: Sumerian farmers used organized irrigation and an agricultural specialized labour force under bureaucratic control. The need to manage temple accounts within this organization led to the development of writing around 3500 BC.

Relations between Egypt and Mesopotamia seem to have developed from the 4th millennium BCE. They began in the Uruk period for Mesopotamia and the Gerzean culture of Prehistoric Egypt, and consisted largely of influences flowing one way, from Mesopotamia into Egypt.

Sumerian farmers grew an abundance of grain and other crops along the valleys of the Tigris and Euphrates. This surplus enabled them to form urban settlements. The world's earliest known texts come from the Sumerian cities of Uruk and Jemdet Nasr.

In Egypt, cylinder seals suddenly appear without local antecedents from around Naqada II c-d (3500–3300 BCE). Their designs are clearly inspired by Mesopotamian ones, and the earliest may even have been made by Mesopotamian craftsmen and sold to the Egyptians.

Cylinder seals appear in Egypt without local antecedents from around 3500 to 3300 BCE, with designs clearly inspired by Mesopotamia. The earliest ones may even have been made by Mesopotamian craftsmen and sold to the Egyptians, before diverging to become more Egyptian in character.
Proto-Elamite influence from Mesopotamia in Susa becomes visible from about 3200 BC. The excavated material of that period allows identification with the culture of Sumer of the Uruk period.

Mesopotamia had been an intermediary in the trade of lapis lazuli between the Indus Valley and Egypt since at least about 3200 BCE. The stone probably originated in northern Afghanistan and had to be transported across the Iranian plateau to Mesopotamia, and then on to Egypt.

culture.text: The Urfa Man, dated to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic around 9000 BC, is considered the oldest naturalistic life-sized sculpture of a human. Göbekli Tepe from the same time has realistic animal reliefs and fragments of reliefs of humans or deities.

At Tell Hassuna, adobe dwellings were built around open central courts. Female figurines have been related to worship, and food was placed inside burial jars, which is linked to a belief in an afterlife.

The Samarra culture is known for finely made pottery decorated with stylized animals, including birds, and geometric designs on dark backgrounds. It was one of the first widespread, relatively uniform pottery styles in the Ancient Near East, and was widely exported.

The Halaf culture lasted between about 6100 BC and 5100 BC, centered on the Khabur River valley. Halaf pottery has been found at Nineveh, Tepe Gawra, Chagar Bazar and Tell Amarna, and at many sites in Anatolia, suggesting it was widely used.

Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Turkey has the earliest known monumental sculptures and circular stone buildings. They date to the PPNA and early PPNB. According to the excavator, they represent the communal efforts of a large community of hunter-gatherers.
Hassuna people made pottery with a cream slip and reddish paint in linear designs. They lived in small villages or hamlets of 2 to 8 acres, and were the first farmers in northernmost Mesopotamia.

The earliest evidence of Mesopotamian religion dates to the mid-4th millennium BC and involved worship of forces of nature as providers of sustenance. Sumerian and Akkadian peoples had been worshipping a mother goddess, Ninhursag, since the Ubaid Period (c. 5500 to 3700 BCE).

At Tell es-Sawwan, evidence of irrigation, including flax, shows a prosperous settled culture with a highly organized social structure. The site belongs to the Samarra culture, roughly dated to between 5500 and 4800 BCE.

The end of Halaf culture was once explained as an invasion by the Ubaidians. Because there is no hiatus between the Halaf and northern Ubaid, most scholars, including Oates, Breniquet and Akkermans, favor a Halafian adoption of Ubaid culture.

At Kosak Shamali, an Ubaid site in northern Syria, spindle whorls, clay scrapers and a clay sealing with a cord impression suggest wool was being produced. The spindle whorls there and at Telul eth-Thalathat II gradually decreased in weight, which could indicate that softer fibers were being spun.
